question: I'm single and only earned $9,000 from a part-time job in 2025. Do I have to file a tax return?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p2 filing requirement table (single under 65: $15,750); Pub 17 Table 1-1
goldAnswer: No, you generally don't have to file. For 2025 a single filer under 65 must file only if gross income is at least $15,750, so $9,000 of wages is below the requirement. Some other situations still require a return (for example, $400 or more of net self-employment earnings), and you may want to file anyway to get back any federal income tax withheld.

question: What does box 1 on my W-2 show?
sourceHint: W-2/W-3 instructions p17 'Box 1—Wages, tips, other compensation'
goldAnswer: Box 1 shows your total taxable wages, tips, and other compensation your employer paid you during the year. It is the federal taxable wage amount, so it doesn't include pre-tax elective deferrals such as 401(k) contributions.

question: Why is the amount in box 3 of my W-2 different from box 1?
sourceHint: W-2/W-3 instructions p17-18 Box 1 vs Box 3 social security wages
goldAnswer: Box 3 shows wages subject to social security tax, figured before payroll deductions, while box 1 shows wages subject to federal income tax. Pre-tax deferrals like 401(k) contributions reduce box 1 but are still social security wages, so box 3 can be higher. Box 3 also leaves out social security tips (box 7) and allocated tips, and it is capped at the social security wage base ($176,100 for 2025).

question: What is the standard deduction for a single filer for 2025?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p25 Table 6 standard deduction chart ($15,750 single)
goldAnswer: For 2025 the standard deduction for a single filer is $15,750 (higher if you are 65 or older or blind, and limited if someone can claim you as a dependent).

question: I earned less than the filing requirement but my employer withheld federal income tax. Should I still file?
sourceHint: Pub 17 p10 'Who Should File'; Pub 501 p5 'Who Should File' – file to get a refund of withholding
goldAnswer: Yes. Even if you aren't required to file, you should file a return to get money back if federal income tax was withheld from your pay; filing is the only way to get that withholding refunded.

question: When is the deadline to file my 2025 federal tax return?
sourceHint: 1040 instructions p8 / Pub 17 p8, p12 'When Do I Have To File?': April 15, 2026
goldAnswer: April 15, 2026, for a calendar-year 2025 return. If you file after that date without an extension you may owe interest and penalties.

question: What does code DD in box 12 of my W-2 mean? Is it taxable?
sourceHint: W-2/W-3 instructions p21-22 'Code DD—Cost of employer-sponsored health coverage'
goldAnswer: Code DD reports the cost of your employer-sponsored health coverage. It is for your information only: the amount reported with code DD is not taxable.

question: Is my scholarship taxable if it only paid tuition?
sourceHint: Pub 970 ch.1 p5-6 tax-free scholarship conditions (degree candidate, qualified expenses)
goldAnswer: Generally no. A scholarship is tax free if you are a candidate for a degree at an eligible educational institution and the amount doesn't exceed your qualified education expenses (tuition and required fees, plus required course-related books, supplies and equipment). It must not be earmarked for other costs, and it must not be payment for teaching, research or other services required as a condition of the scholarship.

question: Part of my scholarship pays for my dorm room and meal plan. Is that part taxable?
sourceHint: Pub 970 p5 qualified education expenses don't include room and board
goldAnswer: Yes. Room and board are not qualified education expenses, so the part of a scholarship used for (or earmarked for) housing and meals is taxable income, even if you're a degree candidate.

question: Which expenses count as qualified education expenses for a tax-free scholarship?
sourceHint: Pub 970 p5 'Qualified education expenses' for tax-free scholarships
goldAnswer: Tuition and fees required to enroll at or attend an eligible educational institution, and course-related expenses such as fees, books, supplies and equipment that are required of all students in the course. Room and board, travel, research, clerical help and equipment not required for enrollment or attendance don't qualify.

question: What is the most I can get from the American opportunity credit?
sourceHint: Pub 970 ch.2 p19 maximum $2,500 per eligible student
goldAnswer: Up to $2,500 per eligible student per year: 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified education expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000. It phases out for 2025 MAGI between $80,000 and $90,000 ($160,000 and $180,000 joint).

question: How much is the lifetime learning credit worth?
goldAnswer: Up to $2,000 per return: 20% of the first $10,000 of qualified education expenses for all eligible students. It can be reduced based on modified adjusted gross income, and there's no limit on the number of years you can claim it.

question: What is reported in box 1 of Form 1098-T?
sourceHint: 1098-E/T instructions p3-4 'Box 1. Payments Received for Qualified Tuition and Related Expenses'
goldAnswer: Box 1 reports the total payments the school received from all sources during the calendar year for qualified tuition and related expenses, minus any refunds or reimbursements of those payments made in the same year. It is not reduced by scholarships or grants, which are reported in box 5.

question: Can I deduct the interest I paid on my student loans, and what is the maximum?
sourceHint: Pub 970 ch.4 p30 up to $2,500, adjustment to income
goldAnswer: Yes, if you meet the requirements. The student loan interest deduction can reduce your income subject to tax by up to $2,500, and it's an adjustment to income, so you don't have to itemize. For 2025 it phases out for MAGI between $85,000 and $100,000 ($170,000 and $200,000 joint).

question: I'm 22 and a full-time college student. Can my parents still claim me as a dependent?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p12-13 / Pub 17 p30 qualifying child age test (under 24 and a student)
goldAnswer: Yes, you can still be their qualifying child: the age test is met if you are under 24 at the end of the year, a student, and younger than the parent claiming you. The other tests (relationship, residency, support, and joint return) must also be met.

question: What is my standard deduction if my parents can claim me as a dependent?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p24 greater of $1,350 or earned income + $450 (capped at $15,750)
goldAnswer: Your 2025 standard deduction is the greater of $1,350 or your earned income plus $450, but not more than the regular standard deduction for your filing status ($15,750 for single).

question: My parents claim me as a dependent. Can I claim my own American opportunity credit?
sourceHint: Pub 970 ch.2 'Who Can Claim a Dependent's Expenses'
goldAnswer: No. If your parents claim you as a dependent, only they can claim the American opportunity credit for your expenses, and expenses you paid are treated as paid by them. You can claim the credit yourself only if no one claims you as a dependent.

question: I'm a dependent with only interest income. When do I have to file a return?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p3-4 Table 2 dependents: unearned income over $1,350
goldAnswer: As a single dependent under 65 and not blind, you must file for 2025 if your unearned income (such as interest) is more than $1,350, or if your gross income is more than the larger of $1,350 or your earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450.

question: What counts as being a full-time student for the dependency rules?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p13 'Student' definition: full-time during some part of 5 calendar months
goldAnswer: You must be a full-time student, as defined by the school, during some part of each of any 5 calendar months of the year, at a school with a regular teaching staff, course of study and regularly enrolled student body (or in certain full-time on-farm training courses).

question: What is the support test for a qualifying child?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p15 'Support Test (To Be a Qualifying Child)'
goldAnswer: To be a qualifying child, the child can't have provided more than half of their own support for the year.

question: If my parents can claim me as a dependent, can I claim someone else as my dependent?
sourceHint: Pub 501 p11-12 dependent taxpayer test: can't claim any dependents
goldAnswer: Generally no. If you can be claimed as a dependent by another taxpayer, you can't claim any dependents. The exception: if the person who can claim you files a return only to get a refund of income tax withheld or estimated tax paid.

question: I made money doing food delivery as an independent contractor. When do I owe self-employment tax?
sourceHint: Pub 17 p10 net earnings from self-employment of $400 or more; Schedule SE
goldAnswer: You must pay self-employment tax (and file Schedule SE) if your net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more.

question: I got a Form 1099-NEC for freelance work. How do I report that income?
sourceHint: Pub 17 p77 Form 1099-NEC fees as self-employment income; p49 Schedule C
goldAnswer: Fees reported on Form 1099-NEC are generally self-employment income: report them on Schedule C (Form 1040), Profit or Loss From Business. If your net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more, you also owe self-employment tax on Schedule SE.

question: Do I need to make estimated tax payments on my side-gig income?
sourceHint: Pub 17 ch.4 p43 'Who Must Pay Estimated Tax'
goldAnswer: Maybe. In most cases you must pay estimated tax if you expect to owe at least $1,000 after subtracting withholding and refundable credits, and your withholding plus refundable credits will be less than the smaller of 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax.

question: Are the tips I get as a server taxable?
sourceHint: Pub 17 p41 'Tips' are part of your pay
goldAnswer: Yes. Tips you receive while working are considered part of your pay and must be included in income on your tax return, on the same line as your wages. For 2025 you may be able to deduct qualified tips (see the no-tax-on-tips deduction).

question: I sell my art online as a hobby, not a business. Is that income taxable and can I deduct my costs?
sourceHint: Pub 17 p76 hobby income on Schedule 1 line 8j; p104 hobby expenses not deductible
goldAnswer: Yes, hobby income is taxable: report it on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j. But you can't deduct hobby expenses: they're miscellaneous itemized deductions that can no longer be deducted, and hobby losses can't offset other income.

question: Is there a new deduction for tips for 2025, and how much can I deduct?
sourceHint: 1040 instructions p6 'No tax on tips' / p101-102 max $25,000
goldAnswer: Yes. For 2025 you may be able to deduct qualified tips paid to you, up to $25,000. The deduction is limited if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing jointly), and you need a valid SSN. It's claimed on Schedule 1-A.

question: I'm on an F-1 student visa. Am I a resident or nonresident alien for tax purposes?
sourceHint: Pub 519 ch.1 p4-7 substantial presence test, exempt individual (student)
goldAnswer: Usually a nonresident alien. As an F-1 student you are an exempt individual, so your days in the U.S. don't count toward the substantial presence test. This exemption generally stops applying once you've been exempt as a student for any part of more than 5 calendar years, unless you show you don't intend to reside permanently and have complied with your visa.

question: How does the substantial presence test work?
sourceHint: Pub 519 p4-5 31 days / 183 days (1/3, 1/6) test
goldAnswer: You meet the substantial presence test for 2025 if you were physically present in the U.S. at least 31 days in 2025 and at least 183 days over the 3-year period 2025, 2024 and 2023, counting all days in 2025, 1/3 of the days in 2024, and 1/6 of the days in 2023. Days as an exempt individual (such as an F-1 student) don't count.

question: What is Form 8843 and do I need to file it as an international student?
sourceHint: Pub 519 p7-8 'Form 8843' for exempt individuals
goldAnswer: Form 8843 is the Statement for Exempt Individuals and Individuals With a Medical Condition. If you exclude days of presence as a student (F-1, J-1, etc.), you must file a fully completed Form 8843, by the due date for filing Form 1040-NR.

question: Which tax return form does a nonresident alien file?
sourceHint: Pub 519 Form 1040-NR
goldAnswer: Form 1040-NR, U.S. Nonresident Alien Income Tax Return.

question: Can a nonresident alien student take the standard deduction?
sourceHint: Pub 519 p39 nonresident aliens can't, except India Article 21(2) students
goldAnswer: Generally no: nonresident aliens can't claim the standard deduction. The exception is students and business apprentices from India who are eligible for benefits under Article 21(2) of the U.S.–India tax treaty.

question: I'm an F-1 student with an on-campus job. Do I pay social security and Medicare taxes?
sourceHint: Pub 519 p61 F-1/J-1/M-1 students: not withheld unless resident alien
goldAnswer: Generally no. Social security and Medicare taxes are not withheld from pay for work authorized for F-1, M-1 or J-1 students unless the student is considered a resident alien. Students enrolled and regularly attending classes may also be exempt on pay for services for their school.

question: Can a tax treaty make my scholarship tax-free as a nonresident student?
sourceHint: Pub 519 ch.9 p65-66 treaty exemptions for scholarships
goldAnswer: Possibly. Many U.S. tax treaties exempt scholarship and fellowship income for students from the treaty country, but the conditions vary by treaty. Check the treaty for your country (IRS.gov treaty texts) and Pub. 901.

question: What is the 2027 standard deduction for a single filer?
sourceHint: Rev. Proc. 2026-35 p13 §4 standard deduction $16,600
goldAnswer: $16,600 for a single filer (or married filing separately) for tax year 2027.

question: What's the 2026 minimum standard deduction for someone who can be claimed as a dependent?
sourceHint: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 p18 greater of $1,350 or $450 + earned income
goldAnswer: For 2026, the standard deduction for someone who can be claimed as a dependent can't exceed the greater of $1,350 or $450 plus the individual's earned income (and not more than the regular standard deduction).

question: What is the 2026 standard deduction for a single filer?
sourceHint: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 p18 standard deduction $16,100
goldAnswer: $16,100 for a single filer (or married filing separately) for tax year 2026.

question: What's the 2027 minimum standard deduction for a dependent?
sourceHint: Rev. Proc. 2026-35 p13 greater of $1,400 or $500 + earned income
goldAnswer: For 2027, the dependent standard deduction can't exceed the greater of $1,400 or $500 plus the individual's earned income (and not more than the regular standard deduction).

question: For 2026, up to what taxable income does the 10% bracket apply for a single filer?
sourceHint: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 p11-12 single table: not over $12,400
goldAnswer: For 2026, the 10% rate applies to taxable income up to $12,400 for single filers.

question: In 2027, at what income does the student loan interest deduction start to phase out?
sourceHint: Rev. Proc. 2026-35 p18 §4.31 Interest on Education Loans
goldAnswer: For 2027, the $2,500 student loan interest deduction begins to phase out at modified adjusted gross income over $90,000 ($180,000 for joint returns) and is fully phased out at $105,000 ($210,000 for joint returns).
